summary:
Mangroove is an open-source web application that transforms radar observations from NASA–ISRO’s NISAR mission into accessible maps of mangrove flooding. It addresses Dancing with the SARs by helping people explore how coastal wetlands change over time.

Our initial study area is the Estero Real delta in Nicaragua, part of the Gulf of Fonseca shared with Honduras and El Salvador. Mangroves support local fishers and shellfish gatherers, but changes to channels can disrupt the water exchange that sustains these ecosystems.

The application combines L-band radar observations, which can reveal signs of water beneath vegetation even in cloudy conditions, with predicted tide levels. It compares flooding during high and low tides in one-hectare cells to identify possible restrictions in water entry or drainage. Interactive maps, timelines, and confidence indicators help researchers, authorities, communities, and the public explore these patterns and prioritize field verification.

Mangroove aims to support conservation and restoration assessments while building a shared, reproducible evidence base for the three countries. Its initial connectivity findings still require validation. With local calibration and field checks, the approach could be adapted to mangrove coastlines worldwide.
details:
Mangroove is an open web application that shows whether the mangroves of the Gulf of Fonseca, Nicaragua, are still “in rhythm” with the tide. A healthy mangrove floods at high tide and drains at low tide. When shrimp-farm dikes, salt pans or roads cut its tidal channels, it loses that rhythm and slowly dies. Seen from above, though, it still looks green.

NISAR’s L-band radar sees beneath the canopy. When water lies under the trees, the signal bounces between water and trunks and returns strongly in HH, while HV tracks the living canopy. Our Python pipeline downloads NISAR L2 GCOV products for a 10 × 10 km area in the Estero Real Delta and calibrates the time series. It then classifies every pass into flooded vegetation, open water or non-flooded, using the wetland inundation algorithm from the NISAR Science Users’ Handbook (section 6.4). Each date is matched with the modeled tide height at the exact overpass time. From this we compute flood frequency at high tide and at low tide for every hectare, and label it as connected, dry (no water even at high tide) or stagnant (water trapped even at low tide). A CUSUM change-point test (handbook section 6.3) flags canopy loss in HV. Results are exported as static files that the web app reads directly.

Benefits and intended impact

The app reveals hidden mangrove dieback before it is visible in optical imagery, and it works through clouds in the rainy season. Protected-area managers can decide where to reopen channels. Producers can show that their farms do not harm the mangrove, and communities get evidence, not just testimony. The Gulf is shared by Nicaragua, Honduras and El Salvador, so one open, consistent dataset supports cross-border management. The method can be applied to any tidal mangrove coast with aquaculture.

Tools

  • Analysis engine: Python with asf_search, h5py, xarray, rioxarray, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, rasterio and pyTMD (tide model).
  • Data contract: JSON Schema.
  • Web app: React, Vite and TypeScript, with Zod, MapLibre GL and PMTiles, deployed as a static site.
  • Other: geojson.io to define the study area. Everything runs on regular laptops.

Creativity

The whole project follows the challenge’s dance metaphor: the tide is the music and the mangrove dances. Our key idea is to normalize flooding by tide height. That turns a standard inundation map into a hydrological connectivity map, with two distinct failure modes (dry and stagnant). The interface explains the radar physics in plain Spanish and English.

Factors we considered

  • NISAR passes at fixed times, so it may miss some tide stages; we report how much of the tidal range it observed.
  • Prop roots and dense mangrove reduce the double-bounce signal, so we use thresholds by canopy height plus per-pixel change.
  • Mudflats can look like open water; interferometric coherence helps separate them.
  • The NISAR record is short, so long-term trends rely on historical L-band data.
  • Every result shows its confidence level and is presented as a hypothesis, never an accusation.
